article.title: University of Chicago UE Members Find AI Conference Valuable
article.content: On Saturday, October 24, six members of UE Local 1103 (GSU-UE), the rank-and-file union of graduate workers at the University of Chicago, attended “Against the AI Campus: Building Power in Higher Ed.” The day-long conference was organized by Higher Ed Labor United (HELU) and held at the University of Illinois Chicago (UIC). The purpose of this conference was to gather workers in higher education together to discuss issues in our workplaces around the burgeoning technology of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and what we can do to protect and expand our worker power. Attendees came from all over the United States and multiple positions in higher education including undergraduate workers, graduate workers, postdocs, non-tenure-track faculty, tenure-track faculty, clerical staff, teaching assistants, operational assistants, and more. The conference began with a discussion defining artificial intelligence, including its history and the recent popular introduction of large language models (LLMs). We discussed how LLMs and other generative AI (GenAI) can be used to degrade or displace our labor in admissions, teaching, research, advising, and evaluation. We then discussed power mapping: tracing through who benefits from the adoption and use of these technologies (the rich and powerful who own the technology) and what pressure points we can use to fight back when we understand these networks of power. We heard from multiple locals who have successfully negotiated language for worker protections related to GenAI into their contracts. The conference concluded with a discussion on how advocacy and legislative action can create real change, especially for public-sector unions. The attendees from UE Local 1103 found many aspects of this conference valuable, especially as we prepare for our upcoming contract negotiations, which will begin in January. The breakout discussions on specific aspects of how GenAI impacts our work (in areas of intellectual property, worker agency, job security, workload, evaluation and discipline, and surveillance) were helpful in modeling discussions we brought back to our own local. Seeing the language other locals won in their contract negotiations provided inspiration for proposals that would unify workers who have very different experiences with GenAI. Worker protections around maintaining the human elements of our relationships with our bosses and our students were especially resonant. Abani Ahmed , a Local 1103 steward in the Computer Science department at the University of Chicago, said, “I really valued hearing from people in all sectors of education, from student to educator and even administration. When thinking about our upcoming contract, it really helped me figure out how to identify the areas that we all agree upon such as the right to refuse the use of AI and the right to have human teachers!” This is not the first time UE higher education locals have participated in discussions on GenAI. In April 2026, leaders from many UE higher ed locals met with staff from the office of Senator Bernie Sanders to discuss how GenAI is impacting our work and how we can protect the dignity of our work in the face of this technology.
